items.headline: Macron speaks of "anger and shame," promises the looters will pay, but declares no state of emergency and offers no new measures
items.lead: President Macron addressed the nation for about nine minutes at 8 p.m. Paris time on 18 October (9 p.m. in Israel), saying, "We all feel anger and shame tonight."
items.text: President Macron addressed the nation for about nine minutes at 8 p.m. Paris time on 18 October (9 p.m. in Israel), saying, "We all feel anger and shame tonight." He blamed the violence of 17 October on "agitators from ultra-left groups, joined by many delinquents" and said "nothing explains it, nothing excuses it"; those who destroyed "must pay," those who looted "must repay," and the state will be "intractable." He said prefects, together with mayors, may go as far as banning some gatherings, ordered "transparency" on the policing strategy and told Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez to "draw all the lessons" on intelligence and anticipation. A crisis cell will help shopkeepers and local governments from Monday. He asked parties and unions to condemn the violence "without ambiguity" and said, "The country needs order... not escalation" and "Our country deserves a fine presidential election in six months." He said he understood high school pupils and students and that a youth consultation platform has received more than 100,000 contributions, but he announced no new cost-of-living measures; the prime minister is to meet parties, unions and local officials. He did not declare a state of emergency, which the right had demanded, and he keeps his trip to four Gulf countries from Monday to Wednesday. France 24, citing AFP, noted that he said nothing about the protesters who were badly injured.

items.headline: Bardella calls the address "lamentable," Retailleau asks again for a state of emergency, Philippe wants decisions; LFI calls it "irresponsible"
items.lead: Candidates on the right and left criticized the address.
items.text: Candidates on the right and left criticized the address. Jordan Bardella (RN) called it a "lamentable address" from a "cowardly and disoriented" government; earlier on Sunday he had said Macron should "ask forgiveness and go." Marine Le Pen, in a televised statement before the address, spoke of "a deep crisis of confidence and authority" and a Macron government "out of breath, exhausted, disoriented," and blamed La France insoumise and "its armed wing, the antifa groups." Bruno Retailleau (LR) wrote on X that the address was "very worrying," that Macron "appears totally overwhelmed," and asked him again to declare a state of emergency. Édouard Philippe wrote on X that he had heard "a laudable wish to restore dialogue" but would have preferred decisions to restore order, saying the country "needs to be led" ("a besoin d'être commandé"). Éric Ciotti said Macron had "spoken to say nothing" and asked the national anti-terrorism prosecutor to take up the case. On the left, LFI's Manuel Bompard called the address "absolutely irresponsible" and Mathilde Panot called Macron an "artisan of chaos"; Marine Tondelier (Ecologists) said she was "very disappointed" that he said nothing about the injured protesters; Fabien Roussel said there were no answers in eight and a half minutes. CGT leader Sophie Binet told AFP that Macron "has understood nothing." Jean-Luc Mélenchon, on LCI on Sunday evening, said a curfew or state of emergency "are not solutions," accused Nuñez and the police chiefs of "total incompetence," and set three demands for Prime Minister Lecornu: a price freeze, the abolition of the Parcoursup university-admission platform and public compensation for the shopkeepers who were hit. Éric Zemmour proposed "remigration" for rioters with dual nationality (BFMTV).

items.headline: Final 17 October toll: 2,397 arrests and 997 police and gendarmes injured; more looting in Paris on Sunday night; curfew for minors in Guadeloupe
items.lead: The Interior Ministry's consolidated count for 17 October is 2,397 arrests and 997 police officers and gendarmes injured, seven of them seriously (BFMTV; RFI), up from the provisional 2,000 arrests and 600 injured given at midday on Sunday.
items.text: The Interior Ministry's consolidated count for 17 October is 2,397 arrests and 997 police officers and gendarmes injured, seven of them seriously (BFMTV; RFI), up from the provisional 2,000 arrests and 600 injured given at midday on Sunday. Looting went on in Paris on Sunday evening: the police made 108 arrests during the day, 66 of them in the evening; at least five shops were looted, including a Darty electronics store in Belleville and two supermarkets; the door of the BHV Marais department store was broken and looters got inside; and barricades were set on fire on the Boulevard Voltaire (20 Minutes, from AFP). Attempted break-ins were also reported in Lyon, Marseille and near Nantes. In Guadeloupe, after looting and fires in Pointe-à-Pitre and Les Abymes on the night of 17 to 18 October in which three police officers were wounded by gunfire, the prefect, Thierry Devimeux, imposed a curfew on unaccompanied minors from 8 p.m. Sunday to 6 a.m. Monday (Le Figaro, from AFP; France-Antilles; Outre-mer La 1ère). In Mulhouse a 17-year-old girl permanently lost her left eye on 17 October; witnesses speak of a tear-gas grenade, and the prosecutor, Nicolas Heitz, has given the inquiry to the police inspectorate (IGPN) (France 3; RTL). According to Le Figaro's live coverage, not independently confirmed: Bordeaux had a record 109 people in custody, 38 of them minors; the Marseille prefecture spoke of 30,000 looters, a figure Mayor Benoît Payan called "far-fetched"; and about 7,000 people, by the city's estimate, marched in Limoges on Sunday evening after the town hall fire.

items.headline: Ifop's Dabi: the riots could strengthen Le Pen's first-round base; no post-riot poll yet; Polymarket steady
items.lead: Frédéric Dabi, director general of Ifop, told AFP on 18 October that the risk of a flare-up six months before a presidential election is "totally unprecedented" under the Fifth Republic; he said the chaos of 17 October could "strengthen Marine Le Pen's first-round electoral base" and make it harder for Jean-Luc Mélenchon to reach the runoff, but urged caution about the effect at the polls (Sud Ouest; Midi Libre).
items.text: Frédéric Dabi, director general of Ifop, told AFP on 18 October that the risk of a flare-up six months before a presidential election is "totally unprecedented" under the Fifth Republic; he said the chaos of 17 October could "strengthen Marine Le Pen's first-round electoral base" and make it harder for Jean-Luc Mélenchon to reach the runoff, but urged caution about the effect at the polls (Sud Ouest; Midi Libre). No poll taken after 17 October has been published yet. On Polymarket (about $153 million traded) Le Pen was at about 48 percent early on 19 October, Philippe 19.5, Lisnard 12, Mélenchon 9.5 and Glucksmann 4.5, almost unchanged from Sunday evening. On Monday the mayors' association holds rallies at town halls at noon, Commerce Minister Serge Papin meets retail federations, banks and insurers, and Nuñez goes to Marseille; on Tuesday National Assembly President Yaël Braun-Pivet is to propose a commission of inquiry, and the Assembly is still scheduled to vote on the first part of the 2027 budget the same day (Le Figaro live; Assembly calendar).

items.headline: First runoff debate: Lula and Flávio trade corruption charges; Flávio admits his father's government fell short on health
items.lead: Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro traded accusations in their first runoff debate, on Band on the evening of 18 October (it began about 15 minutes late and ended about 10:15 p.m. Brasília time, 4:15 a.m. Monday in Israel).
items.text: Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro traded accusations in their first runoff debate, on Band on the evening of 18 October (it began about 15 minutes late and ended about 10:15 p.m. Brasília time, 4:15 a.m. Monday in Israel). Flávio raised the INSS pension fraud and the names of Roberta Luchsinger and Lula's son Fábio Luís ("Lulinha"); Lula raised the Banco Master case and money from its owner, Daniel Vorcaro, for a film about Jair Bolsonaro, and told the Bolsonaros, over Eduardo Bolsonaro's campaign in the United States, "You are betraying the homeland" (Exame). In one exchange Flávio asked whether "60 percent of prisoners voted for you"; Lula answered, "I want 100 percent, including your father." Flávio admitted that health "was not the best result" of his father's government and said, "I make my mea culpa here" (O Globo); he promised a public health service "of Einstein standard," a "war on the PCC as narco-terrorists," a Ministry of Prosperity and a plan to buy household and business debts from the banks. O Globo columnist Míriam Leitão wrote that Lula had the advantage in the second block and that Flávio's debt plan recycles the government's own Desenrola program. In the third block Lula challenged Flávio to open his bank and phone records to the heads of the Supreme Court and the Electoral Court "so that the Brazilian people can find out who the thief is"; Flávio replied, "Your money is always off the books" (Band; CartaCapital). Political scientists quoted by Valor expect little effect on votes, since Quaest found 91 percent and Datafolha 93 percent of voters say their choice is final. On Polymarket (about $188 million traded) Flávio was at about 78.5 percent early on 19 October, down from about 80 on Sunday evening, and Lula at 20.5. New polls registered with the electoral court for release from 19 October include AtlasIntel (13 to 18 October, 5,000 interviews) and PoderData; Quaest is due on 21 October and Datafolha on 22 October. The runoff is on 25 October.

items.headline: Health-tech startup MyMonitor.AI moves its headquarters from Philadelphia to downtown Trenton
items.lead: MyMonitor.AI, a health-care artificial intelligence startup, has moved its headquarters from Philadelphia to Suite 202 at 1 West State Street in downtown Trenton; Mayor Reed Gusciora joined founder and chief executive Charles Mbata for a ribbon cutting on 13 October (Trenton Journal, from a city release; Quadratín).
items.text: MyMonitor.AI, a health-care artificial intelligence startup, has moved its headquarters from Philadelphia to Suite 202 at 1 West State Street in downtown Trenton; Mayor Reed Gusciora joined founder and chief executive Charles Mbata for a ribbon cutting on 13 October (Trenton Journal, from a city release; Quadratín). The company was one of 13 in the first Trenton group of the Novella Center for Entrepreneurship's Conscious Venture Lab, a free 14-week accelerator that began in October 2025. Government role: the accelerator is paid for by a City of Trenton grant from its federal Coronavirus Local Fiscal Recovery Fund money (Community News, May 2025); no public subsidy to the company itself has been reported, and no job numbers were given. The ribbon cutting took place before the last edition but had not been reported here.

items.headline: Grok Bot update: company says computer tasks finish three times faster; The Grid Fin reports X Chat access and new finance connectors
items.lead: The Grok Bot account announced on X on 16 October an update to "quality, polish, and speed": it says computer tasks now finish three times sooner on average and other replies arrive in less than half the time, chat cards have a cleaner design, voice calls are faster and better at remembering past conversations, email supports plus aliases for routines, tagging @bot in an X post starts a task, and notifications go only to the device in use.
items.text: The Grok Bot account announced on X on 16 October an update to "quality, polish, and speed": it says computer tasks now finish three times sooner on average and other replies arrive in less than half the time, chat cards have a cleaner design, voice calls are faster and better at remembering past conversations, email supports plus aliases for routines, tagging @bot in an X post starts a task, and notifications go only to the device in use. The Grid Fin reports that the same update lets Grok Bot read a user's X Chat messages once X is connected, announced by Paul Vann, and adds connectors including Robinhood, Coinbase, Trello, PostHog, beehiiv and eToro; those additions are not independently confirmed here. The company has not said how it measured the speed gain, and the official changelog still lists version 0.70.2 of 11 October as the latest release.

items.headline: Before Tuesday's results, analysts expect SpaceX's first quarterly profit as a listed company
items.lead: SpaceX reports third-quarter results after the market closes on Tuesday, 20 October, with an audio webcast at 4:30 p.m. New York time (11:30 p.m. in Israel); it is the first report to include Cursor, bought in August (TECHi).
items.text: SpaceX reports third-quarter results after the market closes on Tuesday, 20 October, with an audio webcast at 4:30 p.m. New York time (11:30 p.m. in Israel); it is the first report to include Cursor, bought in August (TECHi). According to TipRanks, analysts expect earnings of $0.14 a share, against a loss of $0.09 in the second quarter, and revenue of $12.89 billion, against $7.81 billion; Evercore ISI raised its price target to $275 from $230 on 16 October. The consensus figures come from TipRanks and are not independently confirmed. SPCX closed Friday at $146.03, down 1.7 percent on the day and, by TECHi's count, 15.1 percent below its 6 October close.

baseline: Dates. The Council of Ministers fixed the dates on 1 July 2026: the first round is on Sunday, 18 April 2027, and the second round on Sunday, 2 May 2027. Voters in Guadeloupe, Martinique, French Guiana, Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, Saint-Barthélemy, Saint-Martin and French Polynesia vote one day earlier. The formal decree that convenes the voters has not yet been published; it must appear at least ten weeks before the first round, that is, by about 7 February 2027. If no candidate wins more than half of the votes cast in the first round, the two leaders meet in the second round two weeks later.

Getting on the ballot. A candidate needs at least 500 signed sponsorships (parrainages) from elected officials, chiefly mayors, but also members of parliament, departmental and regional councilors and others. The 500 must come from at least 30 departments or overseas territories, with no more than one tenth from any one of them. The forms are sent out after the decree is published, and the deadline is calculated to fall on about 12 March 2027 (a calculation from the law, not yet an official date). The Constitutional Council then publishes the official list of candidates and the names of the sponsors.
Macron. Emmanuel Macron, elected in 2017 and re-elected in 2022, cannot run, because the Constitution limits a president to two consecutive terms.

Candidates. National Rally (RN): Marine Le Pen, who announced on 7 July 2026 that she will run for a fourth time, with Jordan Bardella as her heir if she cannot. The center and Macron's former camp: Édouard Philippe (Horizons, declared since September 2024) and Gabriel Attal (Renaissance, declared in May 2026). The Republicans (LR): Bruno Retailleau, designated by the party in April 2026; David Lisnard, mayor of Cannes, also declared, in March 2026. Radical left: Jean-Luc Mélenchon (La France insoumise), declared in May 2026. Social-democratic left: Raphaël Glucksmann (Place publique), who won the joint primary of the Socialist Party, Place publique and the Gauche républicaine et socialiste on 11 October 2026 with 66.2 percent. Others tested in polls or declared include Éric Zemmour or Sarah Knafo (Reconquête), Fabien Roussel (Communists), Marine Tondelier (Greens), Nicolas Dupont-Aignan, Nathalie Arthaud, François Ruffin, Dominique de Villepin, the essayist Natacha Polony (declared 14 October 2026), and former president François Hollande, who has not ruled out a run. The month in which Philippe and Attal declared is taken from summaries and is unconfirmed.

Polls. Every recent poll puts Le Pen far ahead in the first round, and the race is for second place, where Philippe, Glucksmann and Mélenchon are now close together. Elabe for BFMTV and La Tribune Dimanche (14–16 October, 1,533 registered voters, published 17 October): Le Pen 31 to 33.5 percent, Philippe 15.5 to 16.5 when he is the only centrist, Glucksmann 15 to 16.5 and Mélenchon 15 to 16; in the second round Le Pen beats Philippe 52.5 to 47.5, Glucksmann 53.5 to 46.5 and Mélenchon 69 to 31. OpinionWay (13–14 October, after the left's primary; 978 registered voters): Le Pen 35 to 37 percent depending on the centrist candidate, with Mélenchon at 14 to 15, Glucksmann at 13 to 16 (up four to five points) and Philippe at 12 to 15 (his lowest in the series); in the second round Le Pen beats Philippe 56 to 44, Glucksmann 56 to 44 and Mélenchon 68 to 32. Ifop-Fiducial for LCI and Sud Radio (12–14 October, 1,390 people): Le Pen 34, Mélenchon 16, Philippe 14, Glucksmann 14, Attal 6 in the central scenario; without Attal, Philippe rises to 18. Odoxa (published 14 October): Le Pen 37 to 38, Mélenchon about 18, Philippe 17. Toluna Harris Interactive (12 October): Le Pen 37, Mélenchon 19. The pollsters differ most on the Le Pen–Philippe runoff: Elabe has it at 52.5 to 47.5, OpinionWay at 56 to 44. No poll yet measures the effect of the violent protest day of 17 October. The Odoxa and Harris figures come from poll aggregators, not from the pollsters' own reports, and are unconfirmed in detail.

Parliament and government. Since the snap elections of July 2024 the National Assembly has had no majority. The National Rally is the largest group, with about 118 to 119 of the 577 seats; the government's base (Renaissance/EPR, Horizons, the Democrats/MoDem and LR) is split and well short of a majority, and 289 votes bring down a government. Sébastien Lecornu has been prime minister since September 2025; his second government survived two censure motions on the 2026 budget in January 2026 (the La France insoumise motion received 269 votes). He presented the 2027 budget on 1 October 2026, again without a majority, and may have to use Article 49.3, which would expose him to a censure vote, or budget ordinances, which have never been used. The Assembly votes on the first part of the 2027 budget on 20 October and on the social security budget on 27 October.

Street protests. Since mid-September a movement chiefly of high school pupils (lycéens), joined by so-called students, unions and others, has blockaded schools and marched over school conditions and then the cost of living; the government accuses La France insoumise of encouraging it, which Mélenchon denies. The national day of 17 October drew 550,000 marchers by the Interior Ministry's count (800,000 by the organizers') and ended in looting in Paris, Lyon and other cities and the burning of the Limoges town hall. The ministry's consolidated toll is 2,397 arrests and 997 police officers and gendarmes injured, seven seriously; one marcher died after collapsing, two teenagers were maimed by police grenades (in Saint-Étienne and Mulhouse, both under IGPN inquiry), and the retail federation counts about 1,500 shops hit. Clashes and looting continued in Paris on 18 October, and a curfew for minors was imposed in part of Guadeloupe. In an address that evening Macron blamed ultra-left groups and delinquents, promised the looters would pay and allowed prefects to ban some gatherings, but declared no state of emergency and announced no new cost-of-living measures; the RN and LR called the address weak, LFI called it irresponsible, and Retailleau keeps asking for a state of emergency. The mayors' association called rallies at town halls for 19 October, the Assembly president will propose a commission of inquiry, and the unions have set an inter-union strike day for 5 November. The government and the right blame LFI, and Mélenchon blames the government's handling; parties from the RN to the Ecologists want the interior minister to resign. Ifop's Frédéric Dabi says the disorder could strengthen Le Pen's first-round base, while other commentators think the far left's promise of street resistance could hurt her; no poll yet measures the effect.

Le Pen's case. On 31 March 2025 a Paris court convicted Le Pen of embezzling European Parliament funds to pay party staff and banned her from office for five years with immediate effect, which would have kept her out of the race. On 7 July 2026 the Paris Court of Appeal upheld the conviction but cut the ban to 45 months, of which 30 are suspended. It ruled that the 15 months to be served had already run since 31 March 2025, so she is eligible. It also sentenced her to three years in prison, two suspended and one to be served with an electronic tag, and a fine of 100,000 euros. She appealed to the Court of Cassation, which suspends the sentence, including the tag. Her lawyers' written arguments were due by 15 October 2026. No hearing date has been set; a ruling is expected before the first round, possibly in early April 2027 (unconfirmed).

quiet_notes.quebec: Liberal members of the National Assembly are sworn in on 19 October; the new cabinet is still due on 21 October.
quiet_notes.carney-case: No new development found; the suspect was last reported in custody in Jordan (23 September). A 6 October FTMQ item repeated July statements by Minister O'Callaghan and is not new.
